title: Clocks
tagline: Year 3 — Angle between hands, overlaps, right angles, mirror images and faulty clocks

introduction.overview: A clock is a circle with 12 hours or 60 minute marks. The minute hand moves 6° per minute and the hour hand 0.5° per minute, so the minute hand gains 5.5° per minute on the hour hand. This chapter uses that relative speed to find the angle between the hands, the times at which they overlap or are at right angles or opposite, and the effect of a clock that gains or loses time.
introduction.placementRelevance: Clock problems are common as short questions in company aptitude tests, often with a direct formula.
introduction.realWorldContext: Scheduling, shift timings and the design of analogue instruments use this angular reasoning.

learningObjectives: Compute the angle between the hands at any time
Find overlap, right-angle and opposite times
Count how often the hands meet in 12 or 24 hours
Handle mirror images and faulty clocks

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A full circle is 360°. The minute hand makes 360° in 60 minutes and the hour hand in 12 hours.

coreDefinitions: Relative speed of the minute hand over the hour hand: 5.5° per minute.
Angle at h hours m minutes: |30h − 5.5m|, reduced to at most 180°.
Hands overlap 11 times in 12 hours and 22 times in 24 hours.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The clock is a two-runner circular race: the minute hand laps the hour hand once every 65 5/11 minutes, which is why overlaps are not at exact minutes after 12:00.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Convert the time to the angles of each hand from 12, subtract, and take the smaller angle. For meeting times, divide the required angle gap by 5.5.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Gain/loss
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Correct time = shown time × (true minutes / shown minutes)

mainNarrative: At 3:20 the hour hand is at 3 × 30 + 20 × 0.5 = 100° and the minute hand at 20 × 6 = 120°, so the angle is 20°. The formula |30 × 3 − 5.5 × 20| = |90 − 110| = 20° gives the same.
To find when the hands overlap after 4:00, at 4:00 the minute hand is 120° behind. It gains 5.5° per minute, so it takes 120/5.5 = 21 9/11 minutes: the hands overlap at 4:21 9/11.
In 12 hours the hands overlap 11 times (not 12, because the 11th and 12th overlaps coincide at 12:00). In 24 hours they overlap 22 times, and they are at right angles 44 times.
For a mirror image, subtract the time from 12:00 (or 11:60). The mirror image of 4:20 is 7:40.
A clock that loses 5 minutes per hour shows 55 minutes for each true hour. If it is set right at noon and shows 3 p.m., the true time is 3 × 60/55 hours after noon, about 3:16 p.m.

deepDiveAspects.title: Time between overlaps
deepDiveAspects.content: The hands meet every 12/11 hours, which is 65 5/11 minutes.

deepDiveAspects.title: Right angle times
deepDiveAspects.content: In each hour the hands are at right angles twice, except at some points where the two instants merge to 3:00 and 9:00.

solvedExamples.title: Angle at a time
solvedExamples.question: Find the angle between the hands at 7:30.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Forgetting the movement of the hour hand.

solvedExamples.title: Overlap
solvedExamples.question: At what time after 5:00 do the hands first overlap?

steps.title: Gap
steps.explanation: At 5:00 the hour hand is 150° ahead of the minute hand.

solvedExamples.title: Mirror image
solvedExamples.question: What is the mirror image of 4:20?

steps.title: Write 12:00 as 11:60
steps.explanation: The mirror image of a time is found by subtracting it from 12:00.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The clock face reverses left and right.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Angle = |30h − 5.5m|; time for a gap = gap/5.5 minutes.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The angle must be at most 180°.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Overlap times are multiples of 60/11 minutes.
